old: The US norm, aligned with the International Yacht Brokers Association (IYBA), is a flat 10 percent of gross sale price, paid by the seller. On a USD 50 million sale, that is USD 5 million. The Mediterranean Yacht Brokers Association (MYBA) sliding scale is 10 percent on the first USD 10 million, 5 percent on the second, 2.5 percent above. On a USD 50 million sale, that is USD 2.25 million. The seller does not always know which is being applied. The buyer almost never knows. The 4 to 5 percent of gross sale price typically captured by the buyer’s broker, paid out of the seller’s commission pool, is the same arithmetic from either base.
new: The US norm, associated with the International Yacht Brokers Association (IYBA), is a flat 10 percent of gross sale price, paid by the seller. On a USD 50 million sale, that is USD 5 million. The Mediterranean Yacht Brokers Association (MYBA) sliding scale is 10 percent on the first USD 10 million, 5 percent on the second, 2.5 percent above. On a USD 50 million sale, that is USD 2.25 million; with the bands applied in euros, the EUR 28 million sale above carries EUR 1.7 million. The seller does not always know which is being applied. The buyer is rarely told. The buyer’s broker is paid out of the seller’s commission, typically half of it or a little less. On the US base that is 4 to 5 percent of the gross sale price. On the MYBA scale it is smaller: about EUR 850,000, or 3 percent, on the EUR 28 million sale.
reason: C4: 4 to 5 percent cannot come 'from either base' when the whole MYBA commission on USD 50 million is 4.5 percent; shares stated per base, working in report

old: None of the structural critique above applies to that work. new: The critique above is not aimed at that work. It is aimed at incentives that travel undisclosed alongside the commission, and at the role ambiguity that asks one firm to answer to both sides of the same transaction. The standard this book applies is written disclosure. A party paid on completion, or by commission, can be engaged, provided the payment, its amount or rate, and who makes it are set out to the buyer in writing in advance, and the party’s role in the transaction is named. The buyer can then weigh the advice against the payment. The independence test in chapter 9 is built on the same rule.

new: The independent adviser is the person the buyer engages first, pays directly, and relies on to act for the buyer across an acquisition, a new build or a refit. This book uses “independent adviser” and “owner’s representative” for the same role. The adviser carries the project at principal level: scope, budget, programme, the contract, and the relationships with brokers, yards and suppliers. The role is not that of a broker, a project manager, a yacht manager or a captain; each of those is part of the team the adviser helps the buyer build. Chapter 5 describes the work on a new build, and chapter 9 sets out how to test and hire the adviser.
